\chapter{Comíamos, Éramos, Íbamos --- Every One With an Accent}
\label{ch:comiamos}
\hlchaptermodality{244}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use the whole imperfect, including all three irregulars.}

I can use the whole imperfect, including all three irregulars.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[comíamos · éramos · íbamos]{comíamos · éramos · íbamos — every one with an accent}

\label{lesson:ES-C63-comiamos}



\begin{quote}
The \emph{-ar} imperfect is whole. Now \emph{comía}, which has had only its singular until now.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the -ía plural}]
Say them: \emph{nosotros} \emph{\textbf{comíamos}}. \emph{Vosotros} \emph{\textbf{comíais}}. \emph{Ellos} \emph{\textbf{comían}}.

And here the accent is on \textbf{every} form, not just one. The \emph{-ía} puts an \emph{i} and an \emph{a} next to each other, and Spanish would ordinarily run two such vowels together into a single beat. The accent keeps them apart, so \emph{comía} stays three syllables rather than collapsing into two.

So the two imperfect sets are mirror images: in \emph{-aba} only one form needs a mark, and in \emph{-ía} they all do.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: and the three irregulars}]
Spanish has exactly \textbf{three} irregular imperfects, and you have had their singulars for a long time. Their plurals:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{ser} & \emph{\textbf{éramos}} · \emph{erais} · \emph{eran} \\
\emph{ir} & \emph{\textbf{íbamos}} · \emph{ibais} · \emph{iban} \\
\emph{ver} & \emph{\textbf{veíamos}} · \emph{veíais} · \emph{veían} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That is the whole irregular list for this tense — three verbs, and now every form of all three. \textbf{The imperfect is complete.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{comíamos}, \emph{comíais}, \emph{comían}
  \item \emph{éramos}, \emph{íbamos}, \emph{veíamos}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many \emph{-ía} forms carry an accent? (\textbf{All} of them.)

And how many irregular imperfects are there in the language? (\textbf{Three} — and you have them all.)
\end{tcolorbox}
